title: Employee Benefits Communication: How to Close the Understanding Gap
summary: Clear employee benefits communication helps employees understand, choose, and use the benefits a company already pays for. TriNet’s 2027 State of the Workplace report found that 80% of employers believe employees understand their benefits while 65% of employees say they do, and this article shows where that gap appears and the steps that help close it. You’ll come away with a year-round communication plan and a short survey for checking what employees understand.
body_markdown:
You've invested real money and real thought into your benefits. Medical coverage. Retirement plan contributions. Paid time off. Life insurance. Maybe an employee assistance program and telemedicine access, too.


And then an employee tells you they don't feel supported. Or worse, they leave for a job with benefits remarkably similar to what you already offer.


What's happening? According to[TriNet's 2027 State of the Workplace report](https://www.trinet.com/resources/research/state-of-work) , 80% of employers believe employees understand the benefits available to them. But only 65% of employees say they do.


That's the widest gap in the report's entire benefits section, and it points to a challenge that's more about employee benefits communication than the benefits themselves. The good news? Employees' overall benefits experience actually improved this year: 68% rated it positively, up five points from last year, and benefits rank among what employees value most when choosing where to work. So much of the path forward is helping people see and use what's already there.


The report surveyed 525 employers and 575 employees at U.S. companies with 5 to 500 employees in 2026, administered by Qualtrics. Here's what it reveals about where the understanding gap shows up, and the steps that can help close it.


## What is employee benefits communication?


Employee benefits communication is the ongoing work of helping employees understand which benefits they have, how to use them, and how to choose among them, from onboarding and open enrollment through major life events and the rest of the year.


The shift that makes it work is moving the focus from what the company offers to how employees experience it. That means thinking about ease of use, fit with real life, and whether people feel encouraged to use what's there.


When employees understand their benefits, they're more likely to choose well, use what they need, and feel supported by what the company provides.

## How well do employees understand their benefits?


About two in three employees (65%) say they understand the benefits available to them, while employers estimate that figure at 80%. And it's not just understanding. Employers rated 36 of the 37 measures in the report's benefits section higher than employees did, which suggests the gap between what's offered and what's experienced runs wider than most leaders expect.


Here's where it shows up.


### How employers and employees rate the benefits experience


The report asked employees to rate their benefits experience across seven key areas, then asked employers how they thought employees would answer. The difference between the two views points to where communication can help most.

Each of those gaps points to a step later in this article.


### What employees know about the benefits they have


Even when a benefit is offered, employees don't always know it exists. According to the report:


- **Medical insurance:** 89% of employers say they offer it; 80% of employees say their company does.
- **Life insurance:** 72% of employers offer it; 60% of employees say their company does.
- **Retirement plan:** 68% of employers offer it; 55% of employees say their company does.


And it gets more specific. 14% of employees are either not enrolled in a medical plan (8%) or don't know which plan they have (6%). A benefit employees don't know about can't help them.


### Why benefits understanding matters for hiring and retention


"Benefits that account for my needs" is now the top consideration for employees looking for a job, at 79%, up six points from last year. Both employers and employees name the same top three[benefits](https://www.trinet.com/benefits) : medical (81% of employees), paid time off (78%), and retirement (77%).


## How to build an employee benefits communication plan


A benefits communication plan sets what employees need to know, when they hear it, and how it reaches them. It doesn't have to be complex, but it does need to be consistent. Here are four steps to get started.


### Step 1: Compare what employees think they have with what the company offers


Start with a short employee survey. Ask which benefits they have, which medical plan they're on, and who they'd ask if they had a question. Then compare the answers with your actual plan list.


The largest misses become your first messages. The report's data points to retirement and life insurance as the benefits employees most often overlook, so those are good places to start.


One tool that can help: a personal benefits statement (sometimes called a total rewards statement) that shows each employee their coverage and what the company contributes. It makes the value visible and gives employees something to refer back to.


### Step 2: Explain each benefit in plain language


For each benefit, create one short summary that covers what it is, what it costs the employee, how to use it, and who to contact with questions. Keep it to one page.


Define the handful of terms that cause the most confusion (deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum) once, in a glossary employees can return to. According to the report, 65% of employees say they have adequate information to make benefit decisions, which means a third don't. Clear summaries help close that gap.


Favor short formats: one-page guides, two-minute videos, side-by-side plan comparisons. The easier it is to scan, the more likely it is to be read. For more on how clear explanations can help, see[how benefits education can help manage healthcare costs](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-benefits-education-reduce-healthcare-costs) .


### Step 3: Set a year-round communication calendar


Benefits communication works best when it's spread across the year, not crammed into the enrollment window. Here's a simple calendar structure tied to your plan year:


When Focus Example Message


First weeks of the plan year


Confirm elections, ID cards, how to find a doctor


"Your new plan year starts today. Here's where to locate your ID card and how to book your first appointment."


Middle months


One resource at a time: EAP, mental health support, telemedicine, preventive care, retirement contributions, HSA/FSA check-ins


"Did you know telemedicine is included in your plan? Here's how to use it." See **benefits already built into medical plans** for more.


Two months before enrollment


What's changing, what to think about


"Open enrollment is coming. Here's what's new this year and how to prepare."


Enrollment window and weeks after


Reminders, then confirmation


"Deadline is Friday. Need help choosing? Call this number." Then: "Here's what you selected for the year ahead."


One more thing: 77% of employees say it's important that the benefits offered to them are personalized to their experience. That means new parents, employees nearing retirement, and part-time staff may each need their own version of your messages.


### Step 4: Use the channels employees already check


Match the channel to the message:


- **Email** for detail and summaries employees can save
- **Text or app notifications** for deadlines and quick reminders
- **Your HR platform or benefits portal** as the one place every summary lives
- **Short manager huddles** for teams on the floor or in the field
- **Printed one-pagers** where email access is limited


Each message should carry one clear next step. "Review your options" is vague. "Click here to compare plans" is better.


## How to help employees choose a medical plan at open enrollment


Here's what else the report found: 36% of employees s


elect the same medical benefits as the year before. Only 19% say they consider which option will be most cost-effective for their health care needs.


That's where you can help. Here's how:


- **Send a pre-enrollment summary** of what changed (new options, cost shifts, coverage updates).
- **Offer side-by-side plan comparisons** with two or three real-world scenarios: a low-use year, a planned procedure, family coverage.
- **Explain how an HDHP paired with an HSA works** if you offer one. For a deeper dive, see[understanding HDHPs and HSAs](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-benefits-communication-education) .
- **Give employees a person to talk to** before the deadline, someone who can answer questions without pressure.


There are reasons[why employees stick with the same health plan](https://www.trinet.com/insights/employee-health-plan-decision-fatigue-benefits-education) year after year, including decision fatigue and habit, and knowing those can help counter those behaviors.


Keep your guidance educational and point employees to plan documents for specifics. You're helping them think it through, not making the choice for them


## How to support employees through major life status change events


According to the report, 65% of employees say their company supports employees well during major life events like parental leave, medical situations, and caregiving. Employers estimate 72%. And parental leave rose most in importance for employees this year, up eight points to 66%.


Life status change events are also when benefits matter most, and when employees are least sure what to do. Here's how to make it easier:


- **List the events that open a benefits change window** : marriage, birth or adoption, loss of other coverage, a move. (For a full rundown, see[life status change event](https://www.trinet.com/insights/whats-a-qualifying-life-event) .)
- **Prepare a one-page guide for each event** with the steps, the deadline window, and who to contact.
- **Ask managers to point employees to the benefits contact** when they hear the news.
- **Check in when someone returns from leave** to make sure their coverage is set and questions are answered.


Change windows depend on the plan and event, so each guide should point employees to the plan documents for timing and specifics.


## How to make benefits help easy to reach


The report found that 64% of employees say they can easily access support for questions about benefits (employers estimate 73%), and 64% find enrollment technology easy to use (employers estimate 71%).


Here's something interesting: benefits information is the on-demand HR service employers most expect employees to want (51%), but only 36% of employees name it, down from 44% last year. At the same time, half of employees (50%) already use AI for questions about benefits almost every time or every time they have one.


The point? Employees need a clear, quick route to an answer. Here's how to set that up:


- **Keep every summary in one place** so employees know where to look.
- **Let an AI assistant or FAQ page support routine questions** like "When does my coverage start?" or "What's my deductible?" 39% of employees think updates and reminders about benefits are better supported by AI.
- **Name a person for personal or complex questions** , the kind that need a conversation.
- **Tell employees which route fits which question** so they're not guessing.


**AI has its place in HR** . But definitely not when it comes to making people decisions that require judgement and thoughtful consideration.


## How leaders can encourage employees to use their benefits


Here's the narrowest gap in the report's benefits section: 64% of employees say they take full advantage of their benefits, and employers estimate 70%. It's also the lowest employer reading among all seven benefits experience questions, which suggests leaders already sense that benefits often go unused.


So how do you encourage use without overstepping? Here are a few ways:


- **Leaders model use.** When a manager mentions (in general terms) that they used telemedicine or took their paid time off, it signals that using benefits is normal and encouraged.
- **Managers mention relevant benefits at natural moments** in one-on-ones. If someone mentions stress, a manager can point them to the employee assistance program without asking for details.
- **The company talks openly about**[mental health resources](https://www.trinet.com/insights/mental-health-support-in-your-workplace) , which often go unused when nobody mentions them. For more on that, see **mental health support in the workplace** .


Leaders share only their own experience, never someone else's. The goal is to make benefits feel accessible, not to make anyone feel watched.


## How to measure whether employees understand their benefits


You can't close a gap you haven't measured. Here's how to check where your own understanding gap sits:


- **Run a short pulse survey** after enrollment and again mid-year. Use agree-or-disagree statements modeled on the report's: "I understand my benefits," "I have enough information to decide," "I can easily get help," "I take full advantage."
- **Before sending it, have leadership estimate the results.** The comparison shows where your company's gap is widest.
- **Track a few supporting signals** : enrollment completion rates, the questions employees ask most, and use of the resources you spotlighted in your calendar.


According to the report, 82% of employers say measuring employee satisfaction with benefits is moderately or extremely easy, so the survey is within reach. The value comes from acting on the answers.


## The benefits you offer may be better than employees think


The[2027 State of the Workplace report](https://www.trinet.com/resources/research/state-of-work) makes one thing clear: much of what employers provide doesn’t reach the people it was built for. And closing that distance often costs less than changing the offer.


The report finds the same pattern in other areas, too, such as **AI guidance and usage** . For example, 90% of employers say they issued AI guidance to employees, but only 66% of employees say they received any.


The benefits your company already offers may be better than employees think. A few clear messages, sent at the right time, can help them see it.

## Frequently Asked Questions


How should benefits be explained to new hires?


In the first week, with the eligibility date, the enrollment deadline, a one-page summary of each benefit, and a named contact. Keep it short and actionable.


A short follow-up after the first paycheck can help answer questions that come up once coverage actually starts and employees see the deductions.


How can a small business without an HR team handle benefits communication?


Make one person responsible, often the business owner, office manager, or a team lead. Reuse summaries and calendar messages from year to year so you're not starting from scratch every time. And lean on your broker, carrier, or HR provider for materials and employee support.


A PEO can help, too, by offering access to benefits along with enrollment tools and ongoing support for employees.
